Maciel , Federal University of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil Lucia Carrera Jardineiro, Oswaldo Cruz Foundation, Brazil Edmundo Gallo, Oswaldo Cruz Foundation , Brazil Abstract: In the so-called “Mosaico Bocaina” region, a territory of high vulnerability in Brazil, the Observatory of Sustainable and Healthy Territories of Bocaina (OSHT), a partnership between the Oswaldo Cruz Foundation (FIOCRUZ), the National Health Foundation (FUNASA), and the Forum of Traditional Communities (FCT) works in the development of social technologies and participatory alternatives that promote equity and respond to the needs of the territory while considering local context and traditional knowledge. Using Praia do Sono, a community in Paraty, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, as a territorial unit, a pilot environme ntal education project focused on ecological sanitation was developed based on the principles of the e cology of knowledge and Environmental Educommunication. The educational process was developed entirely with local agents of the community and changed foll owing the interaction with students. A qualitative methodology (participant observation) was used, and an interpretative analysis was carried out. This paper introduces and analyzes the class plan developed and the creation of a teaching-learning strategy promoting different forms of knowledge of participants, especially students, and evaluating the consequences of the education actions carried out. Keywords: Environmental Educommunication, Ecology of Knowledge, Ecological Sanitation, Traditional Communities Introduction his paper introduces a pilot environmental communication project promoted as a structuring action by the Observatory of Sustainable and Healthy Territories of Bocaina (OSHT). The project is based on educommunication and the ecology of knowledge and has the goal of generating awareness and implementing an ecological sanitation project in the traditional Caiçara community of Praia do Sono, Paraty, Rio de Janeiro. The municipality of Paraty is a priority for cultural and natural conservation , with relevant Atlantic Forest remnants coexisting with traditional communities. The region is under high socio -environmental vulnerability because of climate change, real -estate speculation, predatory tourism and the increasing precariousness of public p olicies. To promote environmental justice and protect the rights of these communities, a social movement was organized by community members to preserve their culture and promote a cooperative and sustainable development model—the Forum of Traditional Commu nities of Angra dos Reis, Paraty and Ubatuba (FCT). FCT fights for the rights of these populations to be in the territory and to maintain their lifestyles and their forms of interaction with nature. Based on the demands of the FCT, a partnership was develo ped with the Oswaldo Cruz Foundation (FIOCRUZ), supported by the National Health Foundation (FUNASA), for the creation of the OSHT. The first step was the participatory creation of a territorialized, counter hegemonic agenda, based on needs expressed by community members. Meanwhile, a series of problems was also discussed through methods such as action research and the ecology of 1 Corresponding Author: Gustavo Carvalhaes Xavier Martins Pontual Machado , Gilberto Cardoso Street, 230/804 Leblon, Psycho-Sociology of Communities and Social Ecology, Federal University of Rio de Janeiro, Rio de Janeiro, RJ, 22430-070, Brazil. email: gustavoxmartins@gmail.com T

knowledge to listen to the needs of the territory from its representatives. The most important issues were identified, and actions were planned in areas like ecological sanitation, agroecology , and community-based tourism. A differentiated education process that strengthens the way of life of traditional communities was also implemented. Actions were planned, coordinated , and supported by a project incubator focused on health promotion and socioenvironmental sustainability (Gallo and Setti 2012). The National Basic Sanitation Plan (PLANSAB), approved in 2013, establishes two major lines of action concerning rural sanitation: structur al and structuring measures. Structural measures involve investments in improving the infrastructure of sewage and drinking water, the promotion of domestic sanitary improvements, and better management of solid waste and storm water drainage. Structuring m easures involve political and managerial support aimed at the sustainability of service provision, including actions related to education and social mobilization and the offering of technical cooperation to municipalities in support of the management and development of projects (Sustainability of Rural Sanitation 2015). However, to account for the needs of some groups, environmental public policies need to include social participation and environmental education projects. This way, effective and efficient actions that are truly incorporated and sustainable and generate equity and autonomy in the territory —some of OTSS’s guiding principles —would be implemented. Sanitation actions uncoupled from educational interventions are unsustainable (Methodological Guidelines 2014). The goal of the ecological sanitation project was to engage and raise the awareness of the community and other actors involved in the process in a cross-cutting, inter-sectoral fashion. The priorities and territorial interventions were established with representatives of the FCT. The environmental education actions were developed together with the implementation of an ecological sanitation system at the Martin de SáMunicipal School at the Caiçara community of Praia do Sono. The school became apilot project because of its importance for the community and its symbolic power.This paper introduces not only partial results of the research project entitled “Sustainable and Healthy Territories:Implementing a Sewage Treatment System at the Caiçara Community of Praia do Sono, P araty, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil,”—financed by Term of Cooperation 10/13 between the FIOCRUZ and the National Health Foundation (FUNASA)—but also partial results of a thesis on ecological sanitation developed by a partnership between FIOCRUZ and the Federal University do Rio de Janeiro (UFRJ). Environmental Education Article 1 o f Law 9.795—of April 27, 1999—which established the National Environmental Education Policy, defines environmental education as a: “process through which individuals and the collectivity develop social values, knowledge, skills, attitudes and competencies related to the conservation of the environment, a good for people’s shared use, essential for health and the quality of life and its sustainability ” (Federative Republic of Brazil 1999, 1). For environmental education to pervade the national educational system and become one of its essential and permanent components, it should be articulated with all levels and modes of ed ucation, both formally and informally, as well as bring the various actors involved in the process together (Federative Republic of Brazil 1999). Environmental education engages with environmental concerns. Its goal is to promote a change in values, attitu des, and behaviors so a new relationship between human beings and nature is established —not a simply utilitarian relationship, but one that recognizes ecological fluxes in an integrated and interdependent manner. Therefore, nature should not be understood only as a “resource” because people cannot be separated from their environments (Moscovici 2007). Current changes demand innovative actions that produce critical citizens that participate and can make decisions that consolidate democracy and promote inclus ive programs. Therefore, all areas of knowledge need to include transdisciplinary approaches of topics such as natural 16

MACHADO ET AL.: ENVIRONMENTAL EDUCOMMUNICATION AND ECOLOGY OF KNOWLEDGE preservation and sustainable development that address natural, technological, social, economic, political, historical, cultural, moral, ethical, and territorial aspects (Gallo and Setti 2014a). In this context, we must address sustainability while considering social, economic , and cultural issues at the same level of importance. Loureiro (2012) states that, in political ecology, no population is considered outside an established territoriality. In other words, the idea of “territoriality” is operationalized to evaluate a group ’s economic activity and its social viability, which need to be within the limits of an ecosystem, a territory (Loure iro 2012). For environmental education to promote social commitment, it must have foundations in environmental justice, equality , and social transformation. As for education, pedagogical processes must be counterhegemonic and applied to social groups in a situation of environmental vulnerability, allowing a contextual, complex, and critical approach. In this sense, environmental education should not only foster ecological awareness in students, but also contextualize the political-pedagogical project to fight cultural standardization, social exclusion, concentration of income, political apathy, and the degradation of nature (Layrargues 2009). Therefore, a study of an environmental education project dedicated to the preservation of ciliary forests and water springs shows that promoting activities in which participants are not only objects of study, but also researchers and producers of knowledge is very important. The use of real-life, practical classes caused students to think critically and promoted a new ec ological and social perspective in them (Melo et al. 2014). Therefore, one of the bases of education must be the promotion of “awareness,” the critical unveiling and the transformation of reality, to develop a human community without oppressors or oppressed (Avila 2014). Therefore, the Methodological G uidelines for Program of Environmental Education in Sanitation for Small Municipalities (PEESSM), financed by FUNASA and implemented in agreement with the National Program of Environmental Education and Social Mobilization in Sanitation (PEESSM), introduces an integrated strategy for the development of environmental education programs/projects in the field of sanitation that includes the participation of the community receiving it (Methodological Guidelines 201 4). Environmental education actions developed in the pilot project at Martin de Sá Municipal School incorporated different communication resources and technologies such as video, radio, and interviews, thus considered environmental educommunication actions. Such actions were based on the PEESSMguidebook and the work done to preserve springs in a rural community (Melo et al . 2014). Environmental Educommunication Educommunication is a form of intervention in education (acting on schools, public policies of other areas, NGOs, etc.) and of technological communication (TV, radio, newspapers, Internet, etc.) aimed at training people and groups in communities to think criticallyand discuss, produce, and disseminate media through participatory collective processes(Carvalho 2009). According to Soares (2002), educommunication is a set of actions aimed at creating and strengthening communicational ecosystems in on -site or virtual educational environmentsand improving the communicational coefficient of educational actions, which are inherent to the planning, implementation, and evaluation of processes, programs , and products. Technological development must be included in education for this interaction between communication and education to be recognized and utilized.Therefore, through actual contact with technology, it is possible to go beyond environmental education, providing students with a critical view on matters and allowing them to assimilate other ways of socially contributing to the world (Soares 2002). Moreover, considering that information is fundamental for education, the new Law of Educational Guidelines and Bases (LDB) opened the possibility of introducing education for communication in the curriculum. Therefore, educommunicators have the role of bringing communication into schools, promoting citizenry and acting as a “professional of articulations” (Soares 2001). Many initiatives in the Mosaico Bocaina area include such actions. A few 17

communication management events that took place in São Paulo —such as “Through the Waves of the Radio” (Educom.radio), whose goal was to train people to use the radio and other means of information in schools —could be mentioned (Soares 2002). In the state of Rio de Janeiro, the “On the Waves of the Environment” program began i n 2007 with the Radio@School project. In 2011, the project was expanded to Mosaico Bocaina. “On the Waves of the Atlantic Forest”— created to serve communities that live close to Environmental Conservation Units (UCs) through radio and audiovisual training workshops and the provision of socioenvironmental information— focused on the Atlantic Forest (Environmental State Secretary 2010). According to PEASPM, educommunication is a methodological strategy to collectively produce pedagogical materials through the painting of pictures, field visits, and group dynamics as well as the production of scale models, leaflets, speaking maps, and more (Methodological Guidelines 2014). The researchers tried to develop a differentiated environmental educommunication approach through an ecology of knowledge, including the various perspectives and forms of knowledge of the territory. Ecology of Knowledge Education needs to recognize the knowledge of each territory to truly include people, who must work as social actors who promote their own awareness. Santos (2008), corroborating this perspective, points to the need of including all varieties of knowledge in a territory and its epistemological, ontological, and cultural diversity. Complexity requires an epistemic opening, which m akes knowledge obscured by hegemonic epistemologies more visible. Therefore, developing a permanent dialogue that articulates modern/scientific/W estern knowledge and native/local/traditional knowledge to form a constellation of knowledges is necessary. The Ecology of Knowledge respects cultural diversity and traditional forms of knowledge, which make learning more inclusive and holistic. Moreover, by recognizing the people in the territory, it fosters autonomy.The learning process, therefore, should not be restricted exclusively to conveying knowledge. Knowledge should be open for discussion and include the interactions with and the cooperation of various actors, stimulating social participation (Santos 2008). Alto (2012) highlights the need for differentia ted and specific education processes in which knowledge is contextualized in the reality of students, through their social experiences and, especially their own culture. Territorialized education strengthens identities. It generates different forms of know ledge, as well as promote s cultural resistance, since rural and traditional peoples normally are denied their rights (Alto 2012). Because they integrate traditional and academic forms of knowledge, environmental education actions are informal and integrati ve and use multiple tools, technologies, and languages (such as video, radio, and interviews) to include local children and actors. Research Methodology It was necessary to act at the level of the territory, that is, considering the territory a living t hing (Santos 2003). Therefore, an integral approach, capable of promoting structural (infrastructure) and structuring (education and social mobilization) ecological sanitation actions was attempted. That approach needed to be not only in line with the culture of the community, but also carried out through an ecology of knowledge, as well as in constant dialogue with the involvement of various actors, surely generating a positive impact. Following Freire’s (2016) critical work . Santos’s (2007) ecology of knowle dge, and Thiollent’s (2011) action-research, the goal of environmental educommunication actions is to stimulate new forms of action that involve individuals in action through a new form of awareness. Through “praxis,” through an action reflection—that is, a conscious action—the goal is stimulating students to be critical thinkers and assume their roles as subjects of their transformation, independent of age (Freire 2016). 18

MACHADO ET AL.: ENVIRONMENTAL EDUCOMMUNICATION AND ECOLOGY OF KNOWLEDGE OTSS uses an integral approach through systemic and integral action research (SIAR) (Morin 2004), which promotes change through the reciprocal transformation of action and discourse through a form of contract (an agreement) that, while formal, is not structured and includes cooperation and participation, allowing for a co- management of theprocess. This approach encompasses the per spectives of Thiollent (2011), Freire (2016), and Santos (2007). Therefore, as highlighted by Santos, “instead of a separation between subject and object, there’s an object which is the subject; instead of a separation between observer and observed, there’s the observer being observed; instead of a separation between thinking and acting, there’s an interaction between both in the research process” (Santos 2008, 141). SIAR is, essentially, a democratic methodology with the goal of promoting strategic changes in successive spirals rooted in the interaction with the living territory and truly considering all the feedback received throughout the process. This methodology demands that researchers become actors (actor -researchers or participant researchers), establishing an effective “ecology of knowledge,” at times pondering, at times acting on the modeling of the phenomenon with the participation of everyone involved (Morin 2004). In this way, it was established during the planning with FCT representatives that the process should start with the Caiçara communities because they were in greater need. Finally, they chose the community of Praia do Sono as a starting point (Gallo et al . 2016). During the development of the clas s plan, academic and community researchers, as well as community members, worked together to find collective solutions by exchanging knowledge and learning from one another. To implement th environmental educommunication strategy at the Martim de Sá Schoo l at Praia do Sono, meetings with various actors in the territory were organized for consultation and collective development. The research was carried out in parallel with teaching/learning activities with an integral and systemic perspective. Different techniques and strategies were used to collect qualitative data. These included participant observation in the development of the class plan; registering the meetings of the team; participant observation during the meetings with students of the Martin de SáMunicipal School; writing reports of meetings with students; organiz ing participatory planning workshops with various actors; registering monthly follow -up meetings between academic and local researchers and with the various actors involved throughout the process; and organizing weekly meetings with the multidisciplinary team dedicated to collective development and consensus decision making, which included the collection of information and the evaluation of stages already implemented. Participant observatio n is a major ethnographic research strategy designed to provide researchers with an intimate approach to a given subject through their involvement with people in their natural territory. It usually involves a range of methods and the observation (with participation) of every moment and form of interaction (Bonatti et al. 2016). The process at the Martin the Sá School was systematized through interpretative analysis and based on the collection of data and the evaluation of results carried out in weekly meeti ngs with the multidisciplinary team (Morin 2004). These were rooted in three dimensions: autonomy, sustainability and equity (Gallo and Setti 2014b). Since the integration of narratives is necessary, the goal is to learn through a dynamic approach that inc ludes the perspectives of local actors and guarantees a reliable balance between practice and theory. Therefore, the journalistic language used connects observations to reality, enhancing research (Morin 2004). The research arrives at its conclusions through logical argumentation and the presentation of facts (Dionne 2007). Data were always triangulated under an integral and systemic approach, contemplating the diversity of views of the actors involved. Triangulation helps researchers to avoid attempting full objectivity, and to recognize that reality can never be fully apprehended (Morin 2004). Based on a systemic view, data were collected through participant observation and the use of a field diary during actions. The process was actively understood, and t he complexity of the interaction between all actors could be observed and presented as results. 19

Since the research project not only involves people, but is also being carried out within a Conservation Unit, once it was approved,it had to be submitted to a nd evaluated both by the Research Ethics Committee of the National School of Public Health (CEP/ENSP) —registration number 1,527,081—and by the Rio de Janeiro State Environmental Institute (INEA) —number 044/014). The Caiçara Community of Praia do Sono Praia do Sono is located within the Juatinga State Ecological Reserve (REEJ), a protected area of around 100 square kilometers in the extreme south of the state of Rio de Janeiro, in the municipality of Paraty. The reserve is part of the Cairuçu Environmental Protection Area (APA Cairuçu), a 338-square-kilometer Federal Conservation Unit created in 1983. The last census was carried out in 2011 and registered 314 native individuals (177 men and 137 women) in the Caiçara community of Praia do Sono. Individuals that were born and raised in the REEJ were considered “natives” or “Caiçara.” Therefore, their sense of belonging and identity is d eeply linked to the territory. Although tourism is currently the community’s main economic activity — followed by sea transportation and artisanal fishing—their culture is preserved by other activities that symbolically represent the territory (Definition of a Category 2011). Water supply and sewage treatment at Praia do Sono is precarious, which is also the reality of various communities in the vicinity. To make matters worse, since it is a tourism region, the significant increase in the floating pop ulation causes problems such aswater shortage, sewage surfacing, and the accumulation of residue. Therefore, the goal of the National Rural Sanitation Program (PLANSAB) is to serve rural populations and traditional communities. It works with the specificities of each territory, which requiredistinct approaches. These approaches are different from those employed in urban areas, both regarding technology and size, as well as the form of management and the relationship with communities (National Plan 2013). In this context, the proposal of a decentralized and participatory scheme strengthens the autonomy and the citizenry of the population served, facilitating the universalization of sanitation and promoting the sustainability of solutions adopted. The goal of OSHT’s Ecological Sanitation Project is to engage the community and the actors involved in the process in a crosscutting and integrated manner. Priorities and territorial interventions were established together with traditional populations. In this context and based on the principles of ecological sanitation, a closed -cycle system for water and nutrients was collectively chosen instead of a linear system. The so-called “Evapotranspiration Tank,” a sealed container, uses the nutrients and water in the sewage, generating products (bananas) and returning the water to the environment via evapotranspiration ( Gallo et al . 2016). The environmental educommunication actions were carried out in alignment with the construction of the first ecological sanitation prototype of the community. Results The discussions and activities offered relevant information for developing solutions and analyzing their impact on students. It should be mentioned that interests of students changed the education project. Results are presented below in greater detail under the following topics regarding the interaction with stakeholders and the community: “ the collective development of the lesson plan ;” “the implementation of the lesson plan ;” and “consequences of soc ial mobilization and conclusion.” Each lesson was considered asa phase of implementation of the program. The data was presented based on the development of lessons with the explicit goal of introducing actions unfolding in the field along with the reactions of students, based on interpretative analysis, to demonstrate the impact and effectiveness of the actions. 20

MACHADO ET AL.: ENVIRONMENTAL EDUCOMMUNICATION AND ECOLOGY OF KNOWLEDGE The Collective Development of the Lesson Plan Based on the premises of educommunication, the lesson plan was developed by OTSS’s Ecological Sanitation and Differentiated Education Teams together with re presentatives of the Caiçara community of Praia do Sonoin a participatory manner. After that, the lesson plan was introduced, discussed, changed, and validated in meetings with education representatives of the Municipality of Paraty (PMP), as well as withthe school teacher through meetings on the field. During technical visits to the school to check information on school users and evaluate educational and construction possibilities, the following information was obtained: morning shift—twenty-three students (six through twelve years of age); afternoon shift—ten students (six years of age); and night shift —seven students (adults). This yielded a total of forty students. After a dialogue with the school teachers and the Secretary of Education, it was decided that the environmental educommunication plan would focus on the morning and afternoon shifts. The goal of the lesson plan for the Martin de Sá Municipal School was to consolidate environmental education, especially regarding sanitation, improving the heal th and the quality of life of the community. As highlighted by Methodological Guidebook for Program Environmental Education in Sanitation for Small Municipalities (PEESSM), the nonlinear and participatory activities were stru ctured in stages, which incl ude diagnostic, planning, implementation with problematization, and evaluation (Methodological Guidelines 2014). To do that, the following measures were attempted: debating Environmental Sanitation and it s relation with different spaces; carrying out integrated practical and theoretical activities that stimulate the “praxis”; planning and developing differentiated education actions based on educommunication with the participation of the children in the local community radio;and using educational videos and promoting a critical reflection in the classroom and/or through other playful activities, such as making posters and writing texts. To support the implementation of the program in the classes, the actions were integrated with the existing networks,involving INEA’s Juatinga Ecological Research team and the Water Surveillance team of the Municipal Government of Paraty (PMP) . In that way, it was possible to promote a joint cleaning effort; carrying out ecological workshops to teach how to make soap from cooking oil; and making recycled toys, always in dialogue with the students, the teacher and the Secretariat of Education of Paraty. The strategy was to carry out weekly activities that were integrated with the daily activities organized by the school teacher. At first, one of the tools used was a mini -diary of the construction so that every student could visit the site every week and write down their observations. Another strategy was to write text or make posters at the end of class with the issues addressed and use it on the community radio, with the goal of promoting the mobilization of the community. Eight open lessons (lectures or practical) were planned to include the participation of all stakeholders involved, discussing the following issues: the water cycle, pollution of water/trash, climate change, waterborne diseases , and environmental sanitation. However, in the perspective of differentiated education and ecology of knowledge, through the dialogue with students, the goal was to carry out and expand the lesson plan, collectively moving according to the perspective, motivations , and interests of students interacting with teachers/facilitators. According to the project schedule (Table 1), fourteen lessons were given. At the end, the following lesson plan had been created after the interaction with all those involved. MACHADO ET AL.: ENVIRONMENTAL EDUCOMMUNICATION AND ECOLOGY OF KNOWLEDGE The Implementation of the Lesson Plan After the lesson plan was discussed and approved by all stakeholders, activities began wit h a “conversation” (a “con versation wheel”) with students to get to know their stories and perspectives on the community. As mentioned by Santos (2008), this conversation was about promoting the value of everyone’s voices and a horizontal perspective concerning different forms of knowledge. During this conversation, the importance of the FCT, the OSHT , and the ecological sanitation project—an innovative project in the region— was explained. Then, the teacher asked students to draw their territory and what they most liked about the community. The importance of the sea and the negative effects of the pollution of the Barra R iver were pointed out by students. After this shared perspective was established, the group jointly decided to visit the region being discussed during their next meeting. At the end of each lesson, even if subconsciously, the critical stance of the children toward their environment was observed in most of the drawings they made, showing that the main river was polluted and improper for swimming. After the children themselves acknowledged the impact of pollution, it was decided that the river would be investigated during the following class. During class two, the children visited the estuary of the Barra R iver. There, the group formed a circle to discuss why the river was dirty. The goal was to stimulate students through the following “generating” questions (Freire 1983): Was the river dirty? Why was the Barra R iver dirty? Will we clean the river? Because of that “research” work—carried out by the group under the guidance of the researchers —they left one side of the river as students and reached the other side as “researchers,” seeking answers for their inquiries. Students wrote notes about the process in their notebooks. Among the various notes they took, they wrote about urinating directly into the river. Such accounts are interesting because they show that kids acknowledge their responsibility in the environmental impact of the community. The fact was used to stimulate the positive and negative effects of the situation, since urine, if used correctly, can be used as a nutrient but can pollute if discarded inadequately. The same approach was used for feces and to explain the idea of a nutrient cycle, crucial for the concept of ecological sanitati on. According to Santos (2008), the ecology of knowledge deals with the phenomenology of moments or types of relationship. Therefore, talking about impacts again with students stimulated engagement and a deeper understanding of local issues. Class three addressed sanitation by comparing sewage and water treatment with our digestive system. Since the issue is very technical and the students are very young, the issue was recontextualized through the local reality, which made students freer to interact. From t he beginning, researchers observed that students had difficulties following the discussions in the classroom. Girls especially had trouble externalizing their views orally. Boys spoke more, mirroring a still mysogynistic structure of society. After this ob servation, the team focused on encouraging the participation of girls, understanding that environmental education involves both ecological and social issues.According to Paulo Freire, the key to the epistemology of the pedagogy of liberation is that no one educates anyone else, nor does anyone educate himself or herself. People educate one another in communion, medi ated by the world (Freire 2016) . This suggests the dialogical, consensual development of knowledge as a possibility in the struggle to overcome the oppressor-oppressed dichotomy (Avila 2014). Therefore, overcoming this duality was also an intention in the classroom, as well as a horizontal participation of both boys and girls. In the afternoon, there was a p uppet show for the younger students (four -to-six-year-olds) about food, which further emphasized the discussion on ecological sanitation. It was a gr eat way of addressing the issue because students interacted with it, participating actively. The interactio n was able to reduce their shyness. During class four, the idea of a water cycle was introduced with the full participation of students. Students volunteered to draw it on the board (Figure 1), exemplifying their perspective on the matter. The participatio n of students was fundamental for their understanding of the 23

phases of the water cycle and of the technology implemented in the school sanitation system : the Evapotranspiration Tank. With that approach, it was easy to understand the use of banana trees in the ecological sanitation station (Figure 2). One of the students explained the entire water cycle in a simple and objective manner. This approach facilitated their understanding, for instance, of what the banana trees did in the ecological sanitation station. The fact that one of the students was able to explain the water cycle in a clear and simple fashion to his colleagues is noteworthy (Figure 2). Figure 1: Students Drawing the Water Cycle. Source: OSHT 2015 Figure 2: Spo ken Map Developed with Stu dents Source: OSHT 2015 A spoken map was also drawn on the board to explain the importance of underground water and the level of care we should have with the territory. The account of one of the students exemplifies this increase in awareness: “If we dump sewage, it goes straight into the ground and pollutes it” (mentioned in the classroom). Based on that, studentstalked about the impact of tourism—especially during Carnaval—at Praia do Sono. The following impacts were mentioned by students: tourists thr owing trash in inadequate places; feces, aluminum cans, cigarette butts, plastic bottles, and bags found along the river; and the low quality of the local water for human consumption (Figure 2). Water quality and the fact that it was impossible to drink it directly from the river were widelydiscussed. Students spoke of Poço of Jacaré, a place where “in the old days, you could drink water straight from the waterfall, but if you do it today, you’ll get sick” (mentioned in the classroom). They alsonoted that this is the best waterfall aroundbut that it is polluted. At Praia do Sono, people drink water after passing it through a ceramic water filter or from purchased water bottles; this issue was discussed as well. The precariousness of the water distribution system—which has many leaks —was also mentioned. Already during the development of the spoken map and the first classes, students showed that they were aligned concerned the care for the territory, as identified by the technical team. Santos mentioned that the ecology of knowledge must seek to promote the convergence of multiple forms of knowledge and of all actors involved (Santos 2008). After that, two videos were screened ( Kauan and the Legend of the Waters 1 and Kauan and the Legend of the Waters 2 ) to promote the value of planning. After the discussion of the films, together with students, the teachers planned a collective effort to clean the beach, the surroundings of the school and the waterfall, so there was actual action carried out regarding what was collectively identified as problems. In class five, given that it was close to World Environment Day, the class discussed “The Water Law,” and students carried out an activity to demonstrate the nutrient cycle and the degradation of the environment. A model (prototype) of the Environmental Treatment Station was built using materials collected from the surroundings by the students. Students were incentivized to play an active role in the process, whether through collecting materials for the model, assemb ling it or registering the activity, each taking turns in each task . Students playfully developed posters and wrote texts in groups, describing what they had experienced, as described by the following account:“The New School at Praia do Sono has fans, a new ceiling, a new fence, a new playground wit h a swing, a slider , and a see-saw. The result of the action carried out at the Martin de Sá Municipal School shows the importance of prioritizing structuring sanitation actions that include environmental education interventions in local schools, stimulating the actual incorporation of general information on the environment and specific information about ecological sanitation, which produced in students a new perspective about themselves, about the world, about their role in the community , and about environmental conservation actions to improve the quality of life. The increase in the participation of students in classes, in suggested activities , and in the communication of the project in their homes and to their families should be mentioned. As classes went by, their initial shyness gave way to participation and an exchange of ideas and 25

opinions. The participation of girls—who, at first, were more timid and reserved—also increased significantly. On the other hand, girls participated more easily in visual and written assignments compared to boys. This apparently mirrors the state of things in the community in which the Martin de Sá Municipal School is, where men generally havemore space to speak than women; these facts were observed from participant observation during the discussion and par ticipatory planning activities. Female participation is reduced in some regions of Brazil, where women cannot fully express their rights and haveto accept conditions imposed by men, as demonstrated in a psychosocial study (Jardim 2014). The following excerpt was extracted from a written assignment of a student of the Martinde Sá Municipal School and shows that the methodology adopted to introduce and discuss ecological sanitation actions at Praia do Sono was successful: “An ecological sanitation system was built in my school. They say it is the first of its kind on the coast. They started digging, plastered it, placed in some pipes, buried them again, planted banana trees on top and told people to go poop.” The fact that the students witnessed the construc tion and did playful assignments to ponder upon it during the process allowed them to truly understand the technology. Class eight was carried out with the participation of the Water Quality Surveillance team (VIGIÁGUA) of the Secretaryof Health of the Mu nicipality of Paraty. The following issues were addressed: waterborne diseases, how to take care of water, building a filter with recycled materials, and the work of a water treatment station, aided by the screening of Clarinha’s Gang and the Water Cycle . A practical demonstration of water treatment deepened and consolidated contents addressed in previous classes, such as the conscious use of water. Class nine, about recycling, addressed the “Rs” of environmental education (rethink, reduce, refuse, reuse and recycle), which were exemplified through the making of ecological toys and the screening of two videos: The Pacific Ocean Trash Island and A Plan to Save the Planet with the Afternoon Gang . The goal was for students to realize that what was previously considered useless waste could be reused. Such practical, playful activities making toys motivated and attracted the interest of students. Carrying out playful activities provided the necessary contextualization for the teaching. According to Moratori(2003), games can be considered an important educational tool, since they integrate the development of the cognitive, affective, linguistic, social, and motor areas and promote autonomy, creativity, and cooperation. Class ten was about climate change and the greenhouse e ffect and included activities that showed how greenhouse gases are formed and the need to close the cycles of byproducts of human activities. It includeda discussion of what c ould be done with the used cooking oil generated in the territory and how it causes pollution. After addressing the issue, it was possible to attract the curiosity of students to jointly develop a workshop for learning how to recycle cooking oil and make soap, which was advertised by Radio@School at the community radio. At the end of the explanation, the film Clarinha’s Gang in the Eye of Global Warming was screened and discussed. At the end, there was a conversation about what could also be done with the oil. Class eleven discussed and developed with students a collective s trategy to mobilize the community and implement Radio@School. All the planning and the discussion of the activities were done with students through the following “generating” questions (suggested by Freire 2016): What should be done? Who will do it? Where will it be done? How will it be done?When will it be done? and Why doing it? To assist the process, the video Why Have a Radio in School? about an experience held in Sorocaba, in the State of São Paulo, was screened. 2 After collectively establishing the goal of creating a school radio, students and the team of FIOCRUZ technicians (OSHT) developed themes for interview s. The chosen issues were w ater, recycling, trash, and ecological sanitation (Figure 8). The “generating” questions created by the students were based on issues they highlighted as fundamental for nature in the community (Freire 1983): Why is it important to take care of the water? Why is it important to save water? Why is it so important not 2 Available at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=med_lRdVndk . [Instead of citing this in a footnote, please cite this in the text and add this source to the reference list.] 26

MACHADO ET AL.: ENVIRONMENTAL EDUCOMMUNICATION AND ECOLOGY OF KNOWLEDGE to litter the beach, the waterfall or anywhere? This class was extremely important because it empowered students through the creation of Radio@School and the critical thinking on different forms of participation with the community. During class twelve, a continuation of the mobilization of the community and the implementation of the Radio@School, students visited the community radio of Praia do Sono to learn the importance of a comm unity radio from a local grio . 3 Grio Zaqueu highlighted the importance of community radio for the people of Praia do Sono, mentioned the services the radio provided since its creation in 2010 , and showed how the equipment works for students to get acquainted with it and better understand the radio (Figure 7). Figure 7: Visit to the Community Radio Source: OSHT 2015 Figure 8: S tudents R ecording R adio S pots about the Environment Source: OSHT 2015 During class thirteen, dedicated to the implementation of Radio@School, radio spots were recorded by students using Audacity (an audio recording software) to later be broadcasted bythe community radio. 4 The following questions sought to be addressed: Why is it important to take care of the water? Why is it important to save water? Why is it important not to litter the beach, the waterfall, or anywhere? At the beginning, students were shy when conducting the interviews. A positive element was the fact that one of the students of the school had already contacted the radio station. She volunteered to broadcast the spots and the advertisement of the workshop to learn how to recycle kitchen oil (Figure 8). This empowered that student and the other girls of the class. Class fourteen was dedicated to teaching how to recycle kitchen oil and making ecological soap. One of the goals was to go out of the school and involve parents and the communi ty. The workshop was carried out in the school yard with the participation and the support of INEA’s rangers. The oil used in the workshop was donated by a community members who owns a kiosk. As pointed out by Melo et al. (2014), the project also provided the contextualization of the practical teaching of parents, students , and community members,which was importantfor students to stop being only passive spectators, allowing a more significant level of learning. Class fifteen finished the first year with a n evaluation of the activities and a participatory planning organized with the active involvement of students. Classes were evaluated through group dynamics and posters were made with the following “generating” statements: “that was good” (high points), “w hat a pity” (low points) , and “how about” (what still needs to be done). There was a closing activity for students to recognize their achievements and receive gifts, stimulating cooperation, and celebrating the process as a whole. The following information was collected from each “generating” statement: 3 Grio means a Caiçara with recognized traditional knowledge. 4 “Spots” refers to audio files for radio broadcasts. 27

• “That was good”—students “thought the workshop to learn how to make soap was cool, because they learned that the oil that makes pans greasy can also become soap and clean pans.” They also liked the activity on water treatment. • “What a pity”—students said they “would like to know other places in the terr itory, to learn more.” • “How about”—students said that “next year, they w ould like to visit other places such as Antigos.” To the question “What do you thin k you can still change at your home?” students replied, “not to throw cooking oil in the kitchen sink and to separate organic and inorganic trash.” At the end of the process, there was a qualitative evaluation with students to recognize the learning throughout the process. Students showed a great level of participation during this evaluation and suggested actions for the following year. To empower students, a second stage of the educommunication project was suggested with a new class plan for 2016 that had the following theme: “Closing the Waste Cycle and Building a School Vegetable Garden.” During the discussion, students provided their opinions and ideas about how to care for their surroundings. Final Considerations The work carried out at the Martin de Sá Municipal School at Praia do Sonowas filled with learning activities, where experiences, knowledge, and personal stories were shared. It was observed that the practices and discussions stimulated actions to be developed collaboratively, listening to andunderstanding the perspectives of students, the community, and the school teacher. It should be mentioned that the goal of environmental educommunication is for students to see reality critically, learning to identify, evaluate , and act upon the elements t hat impact their lives in the different dimensions of sustainability through solutions that promote an increase in the quality of life andkeep the environment sustainable and healthy.Therefore, it is important that authorities, project coordinators , and teams understand the necessary association between structural sanitation initiatives in rural and traditional communities and structuring actions— focusing on mobilization, awareness, appropriation , and stimulation of an active social life —in order for these communities to really take over the solutions implemented. The environmental educommunication program of the Martin de Sá Municipal School at Praia do Sono associated with the construction of an ecological sanitation system caused the community to develop a greater level of critical understanding, including the involvement of students and an active level of participation throughout the entire process. An important point was how children explained the sanitation technology implemented in the territory —an Evapotranspiration Tank—which changed how OSHT’s technical team explain s the technology to communities. Therefore, the program was educationalnot only for students, but also for the technical team, which was able to use the language of the territory and re cognize the best way to introduce issues, critically reflecting on itself and each situation. Through a true ecology of knowledge, the technical team was able to consider the knowledge of all stakeholders involved and allow the construction of a shared wisdom on how to collectively problematize and take care of the territory. It could be observed that the combined use of environmental education and the ecology of knowledge with the true inclusion of all actors is transformative and allows values and cogniti ve patterns to change, strengthening individuals to the full exercise of their citizenry, providing them with a new form of action and allowing them to overcome their obstacles. However, numerous challenges were faced throughout the process. Among them wer e the isolation of the community and the need for sea transportation, which made it difficult for the technical team to get to the s chool and maintain the schedule due to weather changes, which often ma de sea transportation impossible. It was, therefore, c omplicated to keep the schedule of classes that had previously been agreed onwith the Secretar y of Education of Paraty, which caused frequent 28

MACHADO ET AL.: ENVIRONMENTAL EDUCOMMUNICATION AND ECOLOGY OF KNOWLEDGE adaptation of the action plan . However, the issue was r esolved with a constant level of dialogue at each week with the actors involved. Another relevant challenge was to organize the educational process with several stakeholders in the territory, using their expertise and creating synergies for the common good by promoting a critical perspective on sanitation in the territory. However, the educommunication project could only be as encompassing as it was because of the team’s capacity of interaction and articulation, the trust established between the director, coordinators, teachers, students , and the school cook and the constant dialogue between all actors. Structuring public policies that promote the active awareness of people in the territory through shared perspectives is necessary. Therefore, the partnership between institutions that generate knowledge and provide formal education should be stimulated to exchange knowledge and promote the critical awareness of the population on the importance of actively preserving natural resources. Moreover, the qualitative evaluation has shown that the direct and indirect consequences of the actions on the community and the group effectively changed the intelligence of students on ecological matters. Their behavior changed at each moment. That was observed through their greater participation in debates, their engagement in practical activities , and their desire to learn more about sustainability and how to take care of their territory. At a few classes and moments — such as the creation of Radio@School and the drawing of signs to promote the awareness of the community—the increase in the students’ ecological awareness and their will to participate were immediately observed. Activities carried out outside the classroom generated a greater level of participation of students and the community by incentivizing them to look at reality critically like a researcher. Students and community members not only appropriated the territory more, but researchers also learned the real conditions of the territory from them. That was most visibly noticed during the making of the spoken map, where the sources of pollution in the community were raised. Students mentioned the same points observed by the technical team and mentioned by the adults of the community. Students showed a greater level of int erest in practical, more playful activities and in activities carried out outside the classroom, which promote critical thinking by integrating content . These activities produced more interaction and more awareness and changed their attitudes more. Students mentioned the visit to the Barra River, the recycled oil workshop, the construction of the prototype , and the creation of Radio@School as the most motivating experiences. Based on the work carried out together with the municipal government of Paraty, our team was invited to introduce the ecological sanitation project to other schools on Environment Day at an event in the city with activities related to sanitation and sustainability. Therefore, the conclusion is that what made the difference during the dev elopment of the lesson plan was listening to stakeholders and carrying out actions and promoting changes in accordance with these stakeholders. This form of differentiated education, which places the interest of individuals at center stage, empowering them in the learning process, motivating both students and educators (the latter a simple facilitator of the process)—is necessary. Differentiated environmental educommunication for ecological sanitationconsiders the territory and adapts lesson plans to it. The goal is to apply it to other places in the region, always including all stakeholders and stimulating their active participation throughout the entire process. 29

Raíssa de Souza Marinho Mestranda em Geografia pela Pontifícia Universidade Católica do Rio de Janeiro - PUC - Rio. Licenciada em Geografia pela Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro. Resumo O presente artigo tem como objetivo apresentar uma problemática que se vive fruto dos conflitos entre populações ditas “tradicionais” e a forma capitalista de produção do espaço, que carrega consigo, de forma inerente, contradições associadas ao seu proces so de produção. Caminhamos a partir de 3 momento da reflexão: 1) A inauguração da rodovia BR - 101, em seu trecho Rio Santos, como marco da abertura da região sul fluminense para a territorialização do capital turístico - imobiliário e a expansão da produção c apitalista do espaço em Paraty. 2)Abordamos a península da Juatinga, os caiçaras e a Praia do Sono buscando refletir sobre como o lugar, a população e a comunidade vem sendo atravessados pela expansão desse modo de produção do espaço e seus instrumentos de dominação. 3)Nesse momento refletimos sobre o processo de mobilização comunitária realizada pela Praia do Sono durante o primeiro ano da pandemia, que resultou em aproximadamente três meses de fechamento do território realizado de forma autônoma. Abordamo s também as tensões internas que surgem do final do movimento que, passados 2 anos, continuam latentes. O artigo evidencia o sucesso da mobilização, as potencialidades da ação coletiva no território caiçara e, simultaneamente, explicita a tensão interna ex istente, que tem como origem dois olhares, desejos e perspectivas distintas de presente e futuro para a comunidade. La réflexion est divisée en 3 moments : 1) L’inauguration de l’autoroute BR - 101, dans son t ronçon Rio - Santos, comme une étape importante dans l’ouverture de la région sud de Rio de Janeiro à la territorialisation de la capitale touristique - immobilière et à l’expansion de la production capitaliste de l’espace à Paraty. 2) Nous parlons de la pénin sule de Juatinga, des caiçaras et de Praia do Sono qui cherchent à réfléchir sur la façon dont le lieu, la population et la communauté sont touchés par l’expansion de ce mode de production de l’espace et de ses instruments de domination.3) En ce moment, no us réfléchissons au processus de mobilisation communautaire effectué par les habitants de Praia do Sono au cours de la première année de la pandémie, qui a entraîné trois mois de fermeture du territoire effectué de manière autonome. Nous abordons également les tensions internes qui découlent de la fin du mouvement, qui, après 2 ans, restent latentes. L’article souligne le succès de la mobilisation, les potentialités de l’action collective dans le territoire de la caiçara et, simultanément, explique la tensi on interne existante, qui provient de deux perspectives, désirs et intérêts distincts pour le présent et l’avenir dans la communauté praia do Sono. Keywords : Communauté traditionnelle, caiçaras, Paraty, Covid - 19, Résistance. Introdução O presente artigo tem como objetivo apresentar uma problemática que se vive fruto dos conflitos entre populações ditas “tradicionais” e a forma capitalista de produção do espaço, que carrega consigo, de forma intrínseca, contradições associadas ao seu processo de produção. Nosso te xto apresenta dois momentos: o primeiro refletindo acerca da expansão dessa produção capitalista do espaço em Paraty, as transformações no sujeito caiçara e na comunidade da Praia do Sono. E o segundo trata de um acontecimento específico, o fechamento do t erritório realizado pela comunidade durante a pandemia, buscando perceber as tensões que surgem desse processo e que permeiam a comunidade ainda hoje. Trataremos aqui de uma comunidade caiçara localizada em Paraty, a Praia do Sono. Lar de aproximadamente 350 pessoas, a comunidade, que já teve um modo de vida associado às atividades de pesca artesanal e a roça, de caráter predominantemente rural, vem sen do constantemente transformada a partir da expansão da produção capitalista do espaço para o sul fluminense. Desde a década de 70, tendo como marco a inauguração da BR - 101, a região é protagonista de uma narrativa, a nível nacional, de enfoque econômico vo ltado para o desenvolvimento de um turismo e veraneio de luxo, sendo ainda marcada pela chegada de grandes empreendimentos de diferentes esferas. Soma - se a esse quadro o fato de que, desde a década de 90, essa comunidade vem sendo constantemente assediad a por um turismo caracterizado como turismo predatório, pautado no consumo do espaço, na desconexão com o meio e que vem transformando, de forma considerável, a forma que a comunidade produz seu espaço e sua sociabilidade, a partir da expansão da racionali dade privada, individual e urbana. Raíssa de Souza Marinho GeoPUC, Rio de Janeiro, v. 14, n. 28, p. 216 - 2 46 , jul - dez. 2021 da Juatinga, vinculado ao departamento de Geografia da Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro. Se aprofunda em 2019, quando começo a desenvolver meu trabalho de conclusão de curso pensando “A atuação do turismo na produção do espaço na comunidade caiçara da Praia do Sono”. O projeto tem como objetivo trazer maior visibilidade às problemáticas presentes no território caiçara para dentro da universidade, buscando, orientados pela Ecologia dos Saberes (SOUSA SANTOS, 2007), de um lado, construir apoio técnico e intelectual na b usca por resoluções dos conflitos e, de outro, trabalhar a valorização do patrimônio material e imaterial caiçara, buscando o fortalecimento dos sujeitos sociais através do reconhecimento e da valorização de seus conhecimentos tradicionais. Assim como disc utir as novas questões que pulsam no/do território, que está a todo o tempo sob olhar de diferentes interesses, tendo associado a ele um forte caráter de luta e vigília comunitária diante dos jogos de força que ali se impõem. Nos anos que integrei o projet o, buscamos expandir nossa atuação, até então muito voltada para o Pouso da Cajaíba e a Praia Grande da Cajaíba, para a comunidade da Praia do Sono, maior comunidade da Reserva Ecológica Estadual da Juatinga (REJ). A Praia do Sono, além de ser a maior comu nidade em número de habitantes, é também em dimensão geográfica e carrega mais uma singularidade em torno da sua localização: ela é a última comunidade abarcada pela REJ na direção Rio - São Paulo, sendo separada da comunidade caiçara de Trindade pela pres ença imponente e conflituosa do condomínio Laranjeiras 1 . Essa facilidade de acesso faz com que a 1 E sse condomínio, que é um dos maiores condomínios de luxo do país, como é mostrado na pesquisa realizada por De silva (2018) faz parte da ofensiva espoliadora do período da ditadura militar empresarial, que se dá através do uso da força e da violência como método de avanço do capital sobre os territórios, realizando a expulsão de diversas famílias. Sendo essa uma prática realizada tanto pelo Estado, como pelos grupos empresariais envolvidos, numa lógica em que as duas instâ ncias atuam alinhadamente. O condomínio já foi motivo de muitos conflitos para a comunidade e continua sendo ainda hoje, alterando os antigos caminhos comunitários, impedindo o ir e vir dos moradores e querendo ordena - lô a partir de seus interesses. Hoje, mais de 20 caiçaras estão sendo processados pelo condomínio por tentarem passar a pé por dentro dele, caminho historicamente utilizado pelos moradores da Praia do Sono por décadas e décadas anteriormente a chegada do condomínio, que está localizado dentro de unidades de conservação. Sabíamos que isso implicaria algumas limitações para nosso trabalh o, uma vez que durante os feriados, assim como na alta temporada, a maior parte da comunidade se ocupa em função das atividades associadas ao turismo e pouco tempo resta para prosear. Mas nós não perderíamos por esperar! Estar na Praia do Sono nas vésper as de um feriado propiciou justamente que o grupo estivesse imerso na significativa transformação espacial que passaria a comunidade, literalmente, no intervalo de um dia para outro. Entre a aparente tranquilidade comunitária dos dias comuns, o movimento d as ondas e dos pescadores conferindo o cerco 2 , o ir e vir dos barqueiros trazendo suas compras e familiares, as crianças indo e voltando para a escola, o horário pontual da missa, os movimentos cotidianos pareciam se apresentar como eram. Entre grandes mochilas e sacolas de mercado de um lado, barracas e caixas de som do outro, uma movimentação diferente se impunha na com unidade e rapidamente, os caiçaras pareciam sumir daquela paisagem enquanto reapareciam atrás dos balcões. Vivenciar essas transformações espaciais na Praia do Sono, que se manifesta de forma intensa pela já mencionada facilidade de acesso e a variedade e xistente de opções de hospedagem, vivenciar o antes, a chegada do feriado e seu durante, foram acontecimentos que me apresentaram novas inquietações. Temos como intuito analisar esse processo por onde julgamos que ele tem início, a partir da abertura da Rio - Santos e, consequentemente, do sul fluminense para um novo momento no que tange sua produção espacial e a criação de uma finalidade econômica para a região, que passa a existir ass ociada ao turismo e veraneio de luxo, pautados no desenvolvimento do setor imobiliário de influência e com participação de interesses internacionais. Nos interessa perceber como esse processo, ao longo de 50 anos, continua atuando na transformação do modo de pensar das comunidades tradicionais que ali habitam, mais especificamente a Praia do Sono, buscando perceber como essa tensão entre duas formas distintas de pensar e produzir a vida continuam existindo, em constante mesclagem e de cada vez mais difícil distinção. Nos interessa perceber como essas contradições se expressam dentro tanto de situações cotidianas, quanto em situações de crise e urgência. Assim como foi com a chegada da pandemia e os movimentos que dela surgem, envoltos em contradições em tor no de divergências sobre os caminhos a serem seguidos, entre a prevalência da lógica do mercado X a lógica da sobrevivência. Nesse sentido, a problemática da pesquisa se apresenta como a imposição da lógica capitalista na vida cotidiana . Entendemos que e ssa imposição não se dá de forma direta, como se nada do que foi e é inserido nesse cotidiano comunitário fosse desejado. Sabemos que não se trata de situações tão simplistas. Muitos aspectos são desejados, enquanto muitos não o são e cada sujeito viverá e ssas contradições de uma maneira específica, de acordo com sua perspectiva, com seus desejos e intenções. Ainda assim, compreendemos que se enquadre como uma imposição uma vez que se trata de uma racionalidade que chega como uma determinação “de cima” a se r adotada, que feito um vírus, chega sem consultar ou pedir licença, contaminando o pensamento das pessoas, da comunalidade para o individualismo.

A modernidade vem de carro: os descaminhos da abertura da Rio Santos e a expansão da produção capitalista do espaço em Paraty Paraty, município limítrofe entre o estado do Rio de Janeiro e São Paulo, compõe a Baía da Ilha Grande, está inserido historicamente, ao longo das últimas cinco décadas, no contexto das transformações espaciais associadas à expansão da produção ca pitalista no espaço no sul fluminense, ocorridas ao longo da segunda metade do século XX. Localizado entre a serra e o mar, com exuberante mata atlântica, repleto de rios e águas que brotam da fonte, com uma farta riqueza ambiental e cultural, lar de diver sas comunidades tradicionais indígenas, caiçaras e quilombolas, o município tem facilidade de encantar e chamar atenção daqueles que passam por ele. As narrativas geo - históricas em torno de Paraty geralmente se encontram associadas aos diferentes momentos econômicos que o município esteve inserido, integrados às transformações econômicas em seu interior e arredores, sendo uma área que obteve ao longo do tempo, diferentes razões de importância. Como captar hoje esse jogo de forças, que permeia há tanto tempo o território, que já se materializou em tensões e resistênci as de diversas ordens? Essa pergunta nos direciona propositalmente para um mergulho ainda mais fundo, para o que seja talvez o campo mais emblemático de ser revelado: os conflitos que não se materializam . As tensões imateriais que surgem dessa mesclagem, a partir da exposição ao modo de produção capitalista do espaço, que tem como instrumentos de dominação os processos de sedução, sujeição e cooptação . Ainda, e simultaneamente, mesmo seduzidos, sujeitados e cooptados, os sujeitos resistem, numa relação comp lexa entre os “benefícios” e os “malefícios” (em busca de expressões menos totalizantes) da chegada da “modernidade” através das curvas e desníveis que levam os caminhos da BR - 101 a Paraty. A territorialização do capital em Paraty se deu em meio a conflito s de natureza diversas, com muitas histórias de resistência camponesa, caiçara, indígena e quilombola, consistidas na luta pelo reconhecimento do direito de permanência na terra, diante de lutas com grileiros, com o Estado e com o capital imobiliário. A luta contra a colonialidade do saber entra em diálogo com o que propõe a já menciona da Ecologia dos Saberes (SOUSA SANTOS, 2007), que defende o contato e a troca entre as diferentes formas de conhecimento. Um conjunto de demandas e bandeiras de luta que podem ser entendidas, de forma geral, como a luta contra a imposição de um modo de vid a outro. A península da Juatinga, os Caiçaras e a Praia do Sono Localizada em Paraty, na região costeira sul fluminense, a península da Juatinga trata de um recorte geográfico de uma área de Paraty, afastada do centro da cidade. Nessa península, que c arrega ainda hoje um certo grau de isolamento geográfico, uma vez que há lugares onde só se chega através de 2 horas de viagem de barco saindo de Paraty, habitam historicamente diferentes comunidades caiçaras, incluindo a Praia do Sono, que viviam até algu mas décadas atrás, uma dinâmica de vida baseada nos conhecimentos e práticas tradicionais como a pesca, a agricultura e a caça. A área que compõe a Península da Juatinga está inserida em um mosaico de unidades de conservação (UC). Essas UC’s são administra das por diferentes esferas: federal, estadual e a municipal. Ainda que cada UC tenha tido seu contexto de criação, elas foram criadas num cenário de urgência e pressão social frente ao avanço da destruição do meio ambiente e dos distintos modos de vida pre sentes na região, que foram atravessados pela consolidação dos grandes empreendimentos no sul fluminense, como as usinas nucleares Angra 1 e Angra 2, o estaleiro Verolme e o Terminal da Baía da Ilha Grande. Além dos diversos projetos imobiliários voltados para atender um turismo e veraneio de alto padrão, sendo atividades com potencial conteúdos da sala de aula os múltiplos saberes comunitários, assim como tornando a comunidade, em muitos momentos, a própria sa la de aula. Tendo sido designado a cada uma das UC’s diferentes usos, legislações e permissi vidades, as questões que surgem entre elas e a presença dos povos com suas respectivas práticas tradicionais já foram palco de conflitos diversos no território. No caso da Península da Juatinga, temos uma sobreposição de UC’s, entre a APA Cairuçu e a REJ, onde a primeira contém a segunda. Apresentada a Península da Juatinga, devemos nos perguntar: mas quem são os sujeitos sociais que habitam esse espaço? Quem são os chamados caiçaras ? Podemos inicialmente nos apoiar em leituras que realizam um mergulho nas origens do termo caiçara, nos apresentando até mesmo a interessante trajetória etimológica do termo, de origem Tupi - Guarani, utilizado para denominar as estacas que marcavam as aldeias ou que eram postas nas águas para cercar os peixes, sendo mais tarde o nome dado às casas onde são guardadas as canoas, até o momento que passa a ser o nome das populações litorâneas do Paraná, São Paulo e Rio de Janeiro, como presente em Adams (2000). Nesse mesmo artigo nos é apresentada a forte relação entre a formação s ocial do caiçara com os diferentes momentos econômicos das áreas costeiras. Esse contexto específico, abordado por Adams (2000) em diálogo com Diegues (2004), proporcionou um ambiente favorável - com um certo isolamento geográfico e uma mesclagem cultura l de sujeitos com diferentes trajetórias étnicas - à manifestação de modos de vida ligados ao extrativismo e mais afastados da densidade social e tecnológica presentes no urbano. Aqui, apesar de nos adentrarmos na trajetória da Praia do Sono como exemp lo de um processo, é importante reiterar como esse processo, de produção capitalista do espaço, que é aqui analisado de um lado, a partir da territorialização do capital e de outro, a partir das resistências que surgem do lugar , estão inseridas como parte de um processo mais amplo, que se apresenta para além da Praia do Sono, para além de Paraty. Abordar o processo de produção capitalista do espaço nos permite trabalhar com uma rica pluralidade de exemplos, de sentidos globais do lugar, como nos chama

Esse sentido global do lugar pode se expressar (e se expressa) de múltiplas formas a partir das especificidades de cada local, sendo o resultado dessa mesclagem, desse jogo de forças entre o interno e o externo (Santos, 1988), a p reciosidade espacial . Que é o fruto dessa relação, sempre única, que se manifesta entre o local e o global, resultando no sentido de cada lugar. Hoje, mais do que nunca, cada lugar, por mais “local” que seja, vai estar, quase sempre, de alguma forma, impregnado de externalidades, de sentidos “globais”. Nesse sentido, estamos de acordo com Santos (1988, p 105) quando coloca que “Cada lugar tem, pois , variáveis internas e externas. A organização da vida em qualquer parte do território depende da imbricação desses fatores”. Esse aspecto pode ser entendido também para pensar a própria formação étnica do caiçara, como uma mesclagem de diferentes grupos: os indígenas originários, os negros de origem africana que foram trazidos escravizados ao Brasil e colonos europeus. Essa mistura entre distintos grupos étnicos, locais e externos, são a mesclagem que formam o caiçara, esse sujeito múltiplo, heterogêneo, c om saberes acumulados oriundos também dessa mesclagem entre as três origens étnicas. Os sujeitos caiçaras foram por muito tempo entendidos enquanto sujeitos sociais ligados a um modo específico de vida, pautado em sua íntima relação com o lugar em que ha bitam, com conhecimentos passados de geração a geração, através da oralidade, a respeito da vida na terra e no mar. Técnicas de agricultura, conhecimentos sobre diferentes espécies de animais e plantas medicinais, os caminhos de caça e da roça, o mar e sua s relações com os ciclos da Lua, as influências dos astros e das estações sobre o calendário pesqueiro, o conhecimento sobre o tempo “só de olhar para o céu”, o saber fazer compartilhado das casas, das estruturas de pau a - pique - ou o chamado “barreado” - , d a confecção de diversos artesanatos para uso cotidiano, do plantio do aipim, da construção da casa de farinha até seu feitio, da cesta à canoa caiçara, realizada em mutirão, dentro da mata, a partir da retirada de um único tronco, arrastada somente depois de pronta para a areia. Todos esses conhecimentos acumulados de geração em geração através da oralidade e da sociabilidade comunitária específica das pequenas comunidades, ao longo de décadas definiu um modo de vida que se manteve com certa homogeneidade

No entanto, hoje, essas definições não nos bastam mais. Estão limitadas. Ainda que muitos dos aspectos mencionados acima continuem fazendo parte da dinâmica caiçara, não são suficientes para abarcar o conjunto de complexidades que compõem os sujeitos caiçaras atualmente. Tendo o território sul fluminense sido atravessado a partir da década de 1970 por uma série de projetos desenvolvimentistas, os sujeitos que ali habitam foram também, e simultaneamente, atravessados por esses pr ojetos que trazem consigo um modo de pensar específico, pautado pela força do privado, do individualismo e da racionalidade urbana, impactando diretamente os cotidianos das diferentes comunidades. Aqui, ao nos aprofundarmos no exemplo da Praia do Sono, sa bemos estar se falando de uma comunidade caiçara litorânea, com aproximadamente 350 pessoas, composta em sua maioria por pescadores e pessoas que trabalham com o turismo em sua multiplicidade. A ação do externo se materializa no comércio, no capital imobi liário, na mercantilização da paisagem, no turismo e no veraneio e não apenas se materializa, mas penetra as mentes a partir dos fetiches e representações do que é estar inserido nesse modelo. E, inerente a essas materialidades e imaterialidades serão comp reendidas aspectos positivos e negativos na interpretação de cada sujeito, dependendo da exposição e da reação que o mesmo tem frente às investidas do capital, através das sujeições, seduções e cooptações, ou frente aos sujeitos que, ao captarem a disputa de sentidos de que se trata, resistem, cada um à sua maneira. Ou seja, trata - se de uma multiplicidade de possíveis formas de cada sujeito se relacionar com o processo em questão, dependendo de como está envolvido, de como interpreta o processo, de suas int enções, suas ambições e desejos, uma vez que cada um é atravessado de forma diferente em suas subjetividades pela força do externo, pelo jogo das representações, pela capacidade de captar o real. Evidenciamos esses aspectos buscando mostrar como são comp lexas as múltiplas expressões do que representa a penetração do modo de produção capitalista do espaço.

Com a chegada da pandemia uma série de medidas são tomadas a nível federal, estadual e municipal, envolvendo os mais diversos aspectos da vida cotidiana, com a suspensão das aulas nas escolas, universidades, fechamento de comércios e serviços. Diferentes formas de controle sobre o ir e vir são impostos sobre os espaços. Um aspecto fundamental na compreensão do contexto pandêmico, como nos chama atenção Boaventura de Sousa Santos, em seu livro ‘O futuro começa agora:da pandemia a utopia’, publicado em 2021, é entendê - la a partir do viés que: “A pandemia não é uma situação de crise claramente contraposta a uma situação de normalidade. Desde a década de 1980 - à medida que o neoliberalismo foi se impondo como a versão dominante do capitalismo e este foi se sujeitando mais e mais à lógica do setor financeiro - o mundo tem vivido em um permanente estado de crise.” (SOUSA SANTOS, 2021, p 25) Diante do contexto político nacional a atuação do Estado no que concerne o enfrentamento da pandemia teve uma postura um tanto quanto contraditória e, muitas vezes, pode se dizer criminosa. O projeto Raízes e Frutos esteve atento à chegada da Covid - 19 no território, promovendo campanhas de arrecadação destinadas à produção local de máscaras nas com unidades e realizando uma live 7 em agosto de 2020, com comunitários de Trindade, da Praia do Sono e da Praia do Bananal (Ilha Grande), intitulada “Território caiçara, turismo e pandemia”. Na live , realizada durante um dos períodos mais críticos da pandemi a, em agosto de 2020, foram compartilhadas as medidas de enfrentamento que estavam sendo estabelecidas, as dinâmicas das redes de solidariedade entre os territórios e a mobilização em torno das barreiras da vida , como ficou conhecido o movimento de fechame nto territorial realizado por Trindade e pela Praia do Sono. Com as trocas proporcionadas pela live , em que atuei como mediadora, se aprofunda ainda mais o interesse de investigar esses movimentos, compreendendo - os como mais um episódio da resistência caiç ara, envolto em contradições diante das pressões externas e internas que se impunham em múltiplas escalas da vida, sendo um grandioso movimento de resistência, que em seu fim expressa tensões relacionados ao modo capitalista de produção e diferentes perspe ctivas e desejos sobre a comunidade. O fechamento inicialmente em Trindade e posteriormente na Praia do Sono, não foram movimentos homogêneos. Ocorreram em temporalidades e contextos distintos, cada uma com seus desafios e especificidades.
